candidate.title: FRAG-Seq
candidate.scope: The assigned Illumina FRAG-Seq schematic, with separate P1, endogenous 5′P, and T4-kinase-treated endogenous 5′OH lanes leading to cDNA. FRAG-Seq/FragSeq/fragmentation sequencing are naming variants of the one target. The far-left title hairpin is descriptive; the three lanes are components of this assay, not three target methods. Primary evidence is used to interpret end-dependent library entry; platform-specific implementation and the diagram’s polyA label are explicitly distinguished. The cited primary implementation used ABI SOLiD3; an Illumina-hosted schematic alone does not establish a separate platform-specific protocol.

Description, final sentence
evidence.quote: Deep sequencing of the cDNA provides high-resolution single-stranded reads, which can be used to determine the structure of RNA by mapping P1 endonuclease digestion sites.
Because P1 cuts 3′ of an unpaired base, a high cutting score at a site indicates that the upstream base is unlikely to be involved in base pairing or tertiary interactions13.

Briefly, the cutting score is the log ratio of probabilities of observing a break in the nuclease treatment versus the control treatment, after correcting for abundance differences and missing/low-valued data (see Supplementary Note 1 for the exact algorithm definition and Supplementary Note 2 for design rationale).

operations.label: P1 endonuclease digestion
operations.description: P1 cleaves the folded RNA backbone at accessible single-stranded regions, producing fragment ends shown as 3′OH and 5′P. The green/yellow P1 icon is a catalyst, not a retained library component.

operations.information_effect: RNA sequence boundaries acquire a physical association with sites susceptible to P1; susceptibility is the structural readout, not a directly sequenced three-dimensional fold.

method_scopes.rationale: All recorded operations belong to the three-lane schematic for one FRAG-Seq assay. Each parallel route has separate local carry-forward, reverse-transcription, and cDNA-endpoint operations. No pooling is inferred. Primary FragSeq nuclear-RNA evidence resolves the catalogue implementation without establishing a poly(A)-selected or Illumina-specific experimental variant. The retained RNA fragment sequences and boundaries are copied into cDNA. Mapped fragment ends are compared between nuclease and no-nuclease controls to obtain relative cutting/accessibility scores; the PNK route additionally exposes background breaks lacking compatible ends. High P1 cutting scores support an accessible upstream base under the probing conditions, not a complete fold. Fragment-size selection and enzyme accessibility can hide regions; small bulges and interior loops are not reliably revealed, and uniform transcript abundance is not the output. Sequencing and score calculation explain the readout but are not depicted graph operations.

Briefly, the cutting score is the log ratio of probabilities of observing a break in the nuclease treatment versus the control treatment, after correcting for abundance differences and missing/low-valued data (see Supplementary Note 1 for the exact algorithm definition and Supplementary Note 2 for design rationale).
Because P1 cuts 3′ of an unpaired base, a high cutting score at a site indicates that the upstream base is unlikely to be involved in base pairing or tertiary interactions13.

Our method is particularly good at locating stem-loops and hinge regions, producing consecutive high cutting scores in those areas. However, it generally does not reveal small interior loops or bulges.
This is probably because cuts in that region would produce fragments that are outside of the 20-100 base size selection range.
FragSeq will not generate the uniform coverage across a transcript needed for accurate abundance estimates or alternative splicing characterization.
